question: The incidence of type 1 diabetes is increasing, currently affecting over 410 000 patients aged 0-18 in Europe, with about 10 000 new cases each year. It is caused by an autoimmune attack that destroys pancreatic beta cells, which produce insulin. If undiagnosed, it often leads to diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA), with severe clinical consequences such as cognitive impairment in children and higher healthcare costs.

Around 40 % of new paediatric cases present with DKA. The EU currently lacks a pre-symptomatic screening programme, creating inequalities in access to early diagnosis and care between Member States. The Italian Law No. 130/2023 offers a replicable model, identifying the disease in its pre-symptomatic phase through autoantibody detection using advanced non-invasive technologies.
In the light of recent Commission commitments to reinforce common health strategies: 1.
Does the Commission intend to develop an EU-level strategy for the early detection of autoimmune type 1 diabetes, inspired by the Italian model?
How will the Commission support Member States in establishing infrastructure for early detection and ensuring access to timely diagnosis and medical technologies?
How will early detection of autoimmune diseases such as type 1 diabetes be integrated into existing or future EU frameworks on non-communicable diseases, health promotion or digital health?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (9.3.2026) The Commission adopted an EU cardiovascular health plan – the Safe Hearts Plan1 on 16 December 2025, in response to a call for action by Member States2 and the European Parliament3. The plan addresses also diabetes in its scope. Through its flagship initiative on early detection and screening, the plan will promote common approaches to early detection across the EU.

Member States may make use of EU cohesion funds4 to enhance their capacities in providing the necessary services. The Commission also supports Member States in reducing the burden of non-communicable diseases, including type 1 diabetes, under the Healthier Together initiative5.

The joint actions JACARDI6 and PreventNCD7, funded under the EU4Health programme, support Member States in working together on cardiovascular diseases and diabetes, and on health determinants. Member States have EUR 7.3 billion allocated from the European Regional Development Fund across national, regional and Interreg programmes, for investments in health infrastructure, equipment and cooperation across borders.

The Commission plans to address diabetes in the frameworks mentioned above, while respecting the responsibilities of Member States for the organisation and delivery of health services and medical care (in accordance with Article 168(7) of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union). Member States exchange views and knowledge through the Expert Group on Public Health8.
The Commission also supports the collection and sharing of best and promising practices through the EU Best Practice Portal on Public Health9.
